title: Type I-II/II-I vortices from dimension-six self-interaction
authors: A. Alonso-Izquierdo, A. González-Parra, K. Slawinska, A. Wereszczynski, T. Winyard
abstract: We show that adding a dimension-six self-interaction to the Abelian-Higgs or Ginzburg Landau model results in a remarkable and rich structure of multi-vortex solutions. Besides the standard type I (attractive) and type II (repulsive) regimes, separated by the Bogomol'nyi-Prasad-Sommerfeld limit (BPS), we identify two new possibilities: type I-II vortices, which attract at short distances and repel at long distances; and type II-I vortices, with the opposite behaviour. Specifically, within the type II-I regime, multi-vortex solutions form chunks of the Abrikosov lattice or clusters. Conversely, in the I-II regime, axially symmetric multi-vortices are stable; nevertheless, depending on the model parameters and topological charge (winding number), they can be either the ground state or not.
summary: This theoretical paper explores how adding a dimension-six self-interaction term modifies the behavior of vortices in the Abelian-Higgs model. It predicts the existence of two novel mixed-type vortices (I-II and II-I) characterized by different combinations of short-range attraction/repulsion and long-range attraction/repulsion. This work provides a detailed phase diagram for these exotic topological structures.
main_problem: The study investigates the nature and structure of multi-vortex solutions that arise when a dimension-six self-interaction term is added to the standard Abelian-Higgs or Ginzburg-Landau model.
main_result: The inclusion of this interaction introduces novel mixed-type vortices, specifically Type I-II (short-range attraction, long-range repulsion) and Type II-I (short-range repulsion, long-range attraction).
method: The analysis combines asymptotic methods for long-range forces with spectral problem analysis to determine the short-range interaction regimes.
model_or_system: The system is modeled by a modified Abelian-Higgs/Ginzburg-Landau Lagrangian, incorporating a potential term $V$ that includes a dimension-six self-interaction parameter $b$.
key_observables: Long-range interaction energy $E_{int}(d)$, short-range force character (attraction/repulsion), and the binding energy ratio $E_N / E_1$ for multi-vortex configurations.
important_parameters: The coupling constants $\lambda$ and $b$, which define the phase space separating Type I, Type II, Type I-II, and Type II-I regimes.
main_assumptions: The long-range analysis assumes the distance $d$ is much larger than the characteristic scales $l_B$ and $l_\phi$. The short-range analysis relies on solving a complex spectral problem.
figures_summary: Figure 1 maps the parameter space $(\lambda, b)$ to show the distinct vortex phases. Other figures illustrate the physical realization of Type II-I solutions (lattice chunks vs. clusters) and the binding energy dependence for Type I-II solutions.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the modified model and analyzes the long-range force behavior, identifying the separation curve $\mu^2 = u^2$. It then tackles the short-range force via spectral analysis, leading to the classification of the four vortex types (I, II, I-II, II-I) based on parameter space mapping.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter/high-energy theory, the mathematical framework of classifying stable/unstable topological defects based on interaction potentials and spectral analysis is highly relevant to understanding defect dynamics in quantum field theories relevant to AMO physics.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1: Structure of the phases of the vortex solutions. Type I: short and long-range attraction. Type II: short and long-range repulsion. Type I-II: short-range attraction and long-range repulsion. Type II-I: short-range repulsion and long-range attraction. The black dot represents the BPS limit λ = 1 and b = 0. The dashed and dotted-dashed lines correspond to the curves that separate long-range attraction from repulsion, eq. (13). The solid line represents the positive/negative mode separatrix, eq. (14). The dotted line is its analytical approximation.

Figure 4: The binding energies EN/(NE1), where the subscript is the winding number, of coincident zero solutions for type I-II solutions for b = 2.0. For small/large λ higher N solutions are always/never global minimisers. However, nearer critical coupling, there is a critical value of winding Nλ,b for which N < Nλ,b the coincident zero solution is only local which for N ≥Nλ,b it is the global minimiser.
Figure 2: The type II-I regime. Example of the solutions being chunks of the Abrikosov lattice. We plot the local magnetic field strength B of bound states for λ = 1.6, b = −1.2.
Figure 3: The type II-I regime. Example of solutions with larger optimal separation clustering. We plot the local magnetic field strength B of bound states for λ = 0.5, b = −1.6.
